_disclaimer: Unlike the canonical cross-reference set (data/sources/cross_references.txt, ~344,800 links from openbible.info / Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, CC-BY), no open verse-level cross-reference dataset exists for the Apocrypha. The links below were hand-curated by an editor, not drawn from a verified academic index. They are a small, illustrative set of the most commonly cited textual/narrative relationships between apocryphal and canonical books, not an exhaustive or algorithmically-derived list. Each entry's `note` states the nature of the relationship.

links.note: The Prayer of Manasses was composed to supply the prayer of King Manasseh referenced but not quoted in 2 Chronicles.
The Prayer of Azariah / Song of the Three is inserted into the fiery-furnace narrative of Daniel 3 in the Greek text.
Susanna circulated as a narrative addition attached to the Greek text of Daniel.
Bel and the Dragon's second episode parallels Daniel's lions'-den narrative.
The Additions to Esther expand Esther's prayer before approaching the king at this point in the narrative.
1 Esdras retells the closing chapters of 2 Chronicles.
Parallel account of Cyrus's decree.
Both visions describe a great multitude in white robes bearing palms before God's throne; frequently noted apocalyptic parallel.
Parallel eschatological judgment imagery.
Tobit's negative-form Golden Rule ('do that to no man which thou wouldest not have done to thee') parallels Jesus' teaching.
Same Golden Rule parallel.
Shared triad of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving as marks of righteousness.
Wisdom's mocking of the righteous man who calls God his father is a commonly cited parallel to the mocking of Jesus at the cross.
Both texts describe death entering the world through envy/sin.
Both describe the souls of the righteous/martyrs at rest before God awaiting vindication.
Wisdom described as the 'brightness'/effulgence of God's glory is echoed in Hebrews' description of the Son.
Wisdom as the agent of creation through God's word parallels John's Logos prologue.
Sirach's personified Wisdom, self-described as dwelling among God's people, is widely cited background for John's Word-made-flesh prologue.
Sirach's roll call of the famous ('Let us now praise famous men') parallels the roll call of faith in Hebrews 11.
Sirach's invitation to 'draw near unto me... and find rest' parallels Jesus' 'come unto me... and I will give you rest.'
Both teach that forgiving others precedes receiving forgiveness.
Baruch's Wisdom 'found her way' and 'dwelt among men' has traditionally been read alongside John's Word becoming flesh and dwelling among us.

The martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7, tortured while refusing release, are widely recognized as the background for Hebrews' 'others were tortured, refusing to accept release, that they might rise again to a better life.'
Eleazar's martyrdom belongs to the same background cluster for the Hebrews 11:35 allusion.
